🇲🇽🫂 <u>CDMX: THE RIGHT TO CARE GOES CONSTITUTIONAL</u>

Mexico City is writing care into its legal DNA. Mayor Clara Brugada is pushing constitutional recognition of new rights — care, arraigo, early education and guaranteed income from age three — while the capital's human rights commission (CDHCDMX) sets up multi-actor working groups on the right to the city and the right to care. "May caring stop being a destiny imposed on women," Brugada said, "and may we advance toward eradicating the sexual division of labor."
banner: CDMX: RIGHT TO CARE GOES CONSTITUTIONAL

🇲🇽🏥 <u>PUBLIC HEALTH: SPECIALTY CONSULTS UP 60% SINCE 2022</u>

Mexico's public health system delivered 31.7 million specialty consultations in January–July 2026, up from 19.7 million in the same period of 2022 — a 60% jump across IMSS, ISSSTE and IMSS-Bienestar. Growth was sharpest where the federal model arrived: +90% in the 24 states federalized into IMSS-Bienestar, versus 20% in those that haven't joined. "Is the public health system doing better? Yes — it's a great indicator," Sheinbaum said.

🇲🇽🏠 <u>35,500 WELFARE HOMES DELIVERED — AND COUNTING</u>

Infonavit has placed 35,500 Vivienda para el Bienestar homes in 114 developments across Mexico, on the road to 1.8 million this sexenio. The latest delivery: 88 families received their keys in Tlaxcala, a state with a 10,000-home goal. Decades of neoliberal policy turned housing into an asset class; the 4T is turning it back into a right.

🚨🇲🇽 <u>SHEINBAUM TO THE DEA: PICK A LANE</u>

President Sheinbaum called out Washington's double discourse on security: DEA chief Terry Cole publicly praised Omar García Harfuch as a trusted US ally at the IDEC conference in Buenos Aires — while his agency keeps recycling evidence-free insinuations of cartel "links" to the Mexican state. "They recognize the work of García Harfuch, but then they allude to supposed ties," she said. Mexico coordinates. It doesn't take dictation.

The story led Mexican coverage and was picked up from Sydney to New Delhi. US mainstream coverage as of Thursday: zero. 🔍 The last time Michoacán made US headlines this month, it was to pause avocado inspections. An actual cartel uprising gets nothing.

‍PUBLIC BOOKS: "Our Guns Make the Violence That People Are Fleeing" August 20, 2026 | 🟢 📰 MacArthur fellow Ieva Jusionyte on Exit Wounds: over 70% of guns recovered at Mexican crime scenes come from the US. Gun stores in US border states: 9,940. In all of Mexico: two. 🔍 The trafficking emergency at the border runs south. A rare US interview that flips the frame: the violence migrants flee is made in America — and it's a business with a lobby behind it. • "It is our guns that make that violence that people are fleeing" • "Now it's sending the guns. And this is where the demand for drugs is"

‍LATIN TIMES: Mexico Faces Pressure to Match Canada's Tariff Relief in Talks With Trump Administration August 20, 2026 | 🟡 📰 Canada just walked out with auto tariffs cut to 15% and steel/aluminum to 25%. Mexico — three rounds of talks, zero retaliation, deeper security cooperation — is still waiting. Mexican industry leaders say Canada's deal "weakened" their government's we're-better-positioned line. 🔍 The omitted number: 85% of Mexican exports still enter the US tariff-free under USMCA — the fight is over the sectoral tariffs Washington refuses to lift. • "Canada's progress has weakened that argument" — Mexican auto and steel industry leaders • Trump on the Canada deal: "very fair"

🇲🇽🏭 <u>MEXICO'S HEAVY-TRUCK MAKERS TARGET 70% REGIONAL CONTENT BY 2027</u>

Ahead of the fourth bilateral USMCA meeting set for September, Mexico's heavy-vehicle industry is already articulating the jump to 70% regional content value in 2027 — six more points of supply sourced inside North America — while pushing to keep the current rules of origin untouched and to scrap the 25% Section 232 tariff on non-North American content, ANPACT chief Rogelio Arzate told El Economista. Washington debates tariffs; Mexican industry does the homework.
